Brookdale expects $495M-$502M 2026 adjusted EBITDA as RevPAR growth guidance shifts to 7.4%-7.9%
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Brookdale Senior Living (BKD) Q3 2026

Management view

  • "Third quarter adjusted EBITDA met our expectations, while RevPAR growth fell short, directly reflecting slower occupancy growth" (CEO & Director Nikolas Stengle). "We now expect full year 2026 adjusted EBITDA of $495 million to $502 million and are lowering our RevPAR growth guidance to a range of 7.4% to 7.9%" (CEO & Director Stengle).

  • "Our revised guidance also includes a strategic decision to increase our marketing investment in the fourth quarter as well as the revenue and expense impact of the fire at our Clinton, Mississippi community in October" (CEO & Director Stengle).

  • "At the same time, we were able to drive significantly improved performance within our community occupancy bands as the number of Brookdale communities above 90% occupancy increased to 186 communities from 167 in the prior quarter and the count of communities below 70% occupancy decreased to 69 communities from 85 in the prior quarter" (CEO & Director Stengle).

  • "At the end of the third quarter, we completed the previously announced acquisition of 17 communities that we had leased" (CEO & Director Stengle). "We recently announced that we have entered into a definitive agreement to acquire 30 communities that we currently lease" (CEO & Director Stengle). "Upon completion, we will own approximately 80% of our consolidated portfolio" (CEO & Director Stengle).

  • "Adjusted EBITDA for the third quarter was $124.3 million" (Executive VP & CFO Dawn Kussow). "Brookdale residences for the third quarter were $707 million" (Executive VP & CFO Kussow).

Outlook

  • "We now expect full year adjusted EBITDA of $495 million to $502 million and full year consolidated RevPAR year-over-year growth of 7.4% to 7.9%" (Executive VP & CFO Kussow). "On a consolidated basis, this implies fourth quarter RevPAR growth in the high 6% range" (Executive VP & CFO Kussow).

  • "Factors included in this assumption are that occupancy growth remains muted during the fourth quarter" (Executive VP & CFO Kussow). "Rate remains relatively firm in the fourth quarter" (Executive VP & CFO Kussow). "Please note that the updated guidance includes our current estimates of the fourth quarter revenue and expense impact of the recent fire at our 97-unit Clinton, Mississippi community, which is currently vacant" (Executive VP & CFO Kussow).

  • "We remain confident that we can drive durable mid-teens annual adjusted EBITDA growth in 2027 and beyond" (CEO & Director Stengle). "We remain confident in our ability to create durable mid-teens adjusted EBITDA growth in 2027 and beyond" (Executive VP & CFO Kussow).

Financial results

  • "RevPAR for the quarter increased 7.5% over the prior year, which is less than the approximate 8.2% level we anticipated for the quarter" (Executive VP & CFO Kussow). "On a consolidated basis, occupancy increased 130 basis points year-over-year to 83.1% -- on a same-community basis, occupancy grew 50 basis points over last year to 83.6%" (Executive VP & CFO Kussow).

  • "For October, consolidated occupancy was 83.5% and same-community occupancy was 83.9%" (Executive VP & CFO Kussow). "Based on current occupancy trends, we now expect full year consolidated occupancy to come in below 83%" (Executive VP & CFO Kussow).

  • "General and administrative expense, excluding noncash stock-based compensation expense and transaction, legal and organizational restructuring costs declined 15% year-over-year to $36.6 million for the third quarter" (Executive VP & CFO Kussow). "We now expect our full year G&A cost to be approximately $154 million" (Executive VP & CFO Kussow).

  • "During the third quarter, our adjusted annualized leverage improved to 8.3x from annualized leverage of 8.4x at midyear" (Executive VP & CFO Kussow). "Total liquidity declined slightly to $524 million as of September 30, 2026" (Executive VP & CFO Kussow). "As a result, Brookdale has no mortgage debt maturities until 2028" (Executive VP & CFO Kussow).

Q&A

  • Brian Tanquilut, Jefferies: asked about why occupancy has been “soft” and the cadence into next year; CEO Stengle: "we have gone through a lot of changes" and "there's some macroeconomic drag" and "leads coming from external sources in general are down this year" while "we're leaning in with Margaret Cabell as our Chief Sales Officer" and "part of our guide down for Q4 is this idea that we're going to spend a bit more money on marketing" (CEO & Director Stengle).

  • Brian Tanquilut, Jefferies: asked about sustainability of labor and marketing expense; CEO Stengle: "we very deliberately adjusted our labor, and it is enduring. It is sustainable" (CEO & Director Stengle); CFO Kussow: "it is really a nominal dollar amount to the year overall" and "I wouldn't think about that coming into and impacting 2027 significantly" (Executive VP & CFO Kussow).

  • Andrew Mok, Barclays: asked to walk through the guidance reduction and fire impact; CFO Kussow: "We brought down our guide mainly due to the pull-through of the third quarter occupancy" and "The fire impacted our occupancy" and "it is a few million dollars in the fourth quarter" (Executive VP & CFO Kussow).

  • Andrew Mok, Barclays: asked if macro/affordability changes pricing strategy; CEO Stengle: "the short answer is no" and "we are anticipating another meaningful in-place rate increase" (CEO & Director Stengle).

  • Benjamin Hendrix, RBC Capital Markets: asked about lead conversion by source and whether higher marketing creates upside; CEO Stengle: "internally generated leads convert more highly" and "The upside is how can we continue changing that behavior" (CEO & Director Stengle).

Sentiment analysis

  • Analysts slightly negative: "Sorry to hear about the facility that burned down" and "given the trend that we've seen all year" (Brian Tanquilut, Jefferies) and "There's a few moving pieces in the updated guidance" (Andrew Mok, Barclays).

  • Management slightly positive in framing but acknowledges pressure: "we are not pleased with our occupancy" alongside "we remain confident" (CEO & Director Stengle) and "third quarter adjusted EBITDA met our expectations, but occupancy and RevPAR growth fell short" (Executive VP & CFO Kussow).

  • Versus last quarter, management language became more cautious on near-term trajectory: in Q2 management said it "reaffirm"ed "2026 annual guidance of 8% to 9% RevPAR growth and adjusted EBITDA in the range of $502 million to $516 million" (CEO & Director Stengle), while in Q3 it said it is "lowering our RevPAR growth guidance" and now expects "$495 million to $502 million" adjusted EBITDA (CEO & Director Stengle).

Quarter-over-quarter comparison

  • Guidance stance shifted from reaffirmation to reduction: Q2 stated "We also remain on-track to deliver on our 2026 annual guidance of 8% to 9% RevPAR growth and adjusted EBITDA in the range of $502 million to $516 million" (CEO & Director Stengle); Q3 stated "We now expect full year 2026 adjusted EBITDA of $495 million to $502 million and are lowering our RevPAR growth guidance to a range of 7.4% to 7.9%" (CEO & Director Stengle).

  • The occupancy narrative moved from early-summer momentum to peak-season shortfall: Q2 said "July occupancy marked a strong acceleration" (CEO & Director Stengle), while Q3 said "that weaker-than-expected occupancy growth during the summer selling season will negatively impact our fourth quarter and full-year performance" (CEO & Director Stengle).

  • Portfolio actions advanced: Q2 discussed a "planned acquisition of 17 communities" expected to close in Q4 (CEO & Director Stengle); Q3 stated "we completed" that acquisition and added a definitive agreement to acquire "30 communities" plus a lease amendment affecting "an additional 39" leased communities (CEO & Director Stengle).

Risks and concerns

  • "Occupancy growth remains our greatest operating challenge and the primary reason for our lower full year outlook" (CEO & Director Stengle). "Lead volume during the quarter was below where it needed to be" and "the lead volume from external sources has declined across the industry" (CEO & Director Stengle).

  • "Please note that the updated guidance includes our current estimates of the fourth quarter revenue and expense impact of the recent fire at our 97-unit Clinton, Mississippi community" (Executive VP & CFO Kussow). "We've incurred elevated consulting and operating costs as we continue to improve the system's efficiency" related to the "2025 ERP implementation" (Executive VP & CFO Kussow).

Final takeaway

Management tied the 2026 guidance reduction to slower-than-expected occupancy growth during the peak summer selling season, including weaker lead volume—particularly from external lead sources—while describing a near-term marketing increase, ongoing cost actions (notably in administrative labor), and the fourth-quarter financial impact from the Clinton, Mississippi fire; alongside the reset, management emphasized continued portfolio repositioning through completed and pending leased-to-owned transactions intended to raise ownership to about 80% of the portfolio and reiterated confidence in “durable mid-teens” adjusted EBITDA growth in 2027 and beyond.

data.title: Willdan outlines preliminary 2027 targets including $1B contract revenue and $140M+ EBITDA following Mantis close
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Willdan Group (WLDN) Q3 2026

Management View

  • "We had a strong operational performance in Q3" and "contract revenue and net revenue each grew 18% to $215 million and $112 million, respectively," with "organic net revenue growth" of "12%" and "a stronger 17% in our Energy segment" (CEO Michael Bieber).
  • "Two important things have happened since our last call" including "on October 30, we closed the acquisition of Mantis Innovation" and "we are raising our full year 2026 targets again" while also "introducing preliminary 2027 targets that call for continued double-digit growth" (CEO Bieber).
  • "Just 2 years ago, commercial work was about 7% of our business. Today, it's about 1/4 of our work" and "with Burton and Mantis acquisitions on a full year pro forma basis, commercial work is equally balanced with work for state and local governments and utilities" (CEO Bieber).
  • "In 2026, Mantis is expected to generate about $120 million in contract revenue" but "we now expect Mantis to add about $75 million in net revenue, not the $120 million as previously communicated" and "that change also means that Mantis' margin will be accretive to Willdan's" (CEO Bieber).
  • "We delivered another strong quarter with net revenue up 18% and adjusted EBITDA up 22%" and "even after deploying $56 million for acquisitions this year, we ended the quarter at 0.2x net leverage" (Executive VP & CFO Creighton Early).

Outlook

  • "We now expect net revenue of $435 million to $445 million" and "adjusted EBITDA of $109 million to $111 million" and "adjusted diluted earnings per share of $5.15 to $5.25" for 2026, with the outlook assuming "approximately 15.9 million diluted shares" and "a 0% effective tax rate for the year on GAAP earnings" (EVP & CFO Early).
  • "We think this picture will come together in 2027 such that for the first time in the company's history, we will achieve $1 billion in contract revenue" and "more than $0.5 billion in net revenue" and "more than $140 million in EBITDA for 2027" (CEO Bieber).
  • Compared with the prior quarter’s raised 2026 targets (net revenue $415 million to $430 million; adjusted EBITDA $103 million to $107 million; adjusted diluted EPS $5.00 to $5.15), management increased each 2026 target range again after closing Mantis (EVP & CFO Early, Q2 vs. Q3).

Financial Results

  • "Gross profit grew 23% to $82.5 million and gross margin expanded about 150 basis points to 38.4% of contract revenue" driven by "a favorable revenue mix, including higher incentive revenue under some of our utility programs and increasing revenue from our LADWP Street Lighting Project" (EVP & CFO Early).
  • "G&A expenses increased 27% to $66.1 million" and stock compensation "rising 58% to $5.0 million" while "depreciation and amortization" increased "48% to $5.8 million" (EVP & CFO Early).
  • "Net income was $11.9 million or $0.76 per diluted share" and "adjusted earnings per share was $1.20"; management attributed the year-over-year adjusted EPS dynamic to "the higher tax rate" offsetting "22% growth in adjusted EBITDA" (EVP & CFO Early).
  • "Operating cash flow was $32.9 million" year-to-date, reflecting "a temporary working capital lag in September expected to reverse in Q4," and "over the last 12 months, free cash flow was $64.5 million or $4.17 per share" (EVP & CFO Early).

Q&A

  • Craig Irwin, ROTH Capital Partners: asked about data center expectations embedded in 2027 targets and resource flexibility; CEO Bieber replied, "demand for these data centers is not wavering" and "our pipeline goes out past 2029" and "we're not expecting any major changes in the data center world."
  • Craig Irwin, ROTH Capital Partners: asked how well Willdan and Mantis fit for cross-selling; CEO Bieber answered, "We think there's a great opportunity here for cross-selling" and "There's essentially no overlap" in client lists.
  • Craig Irwin, ROTH Capital Partners: asked whether free cash flow should track EBITDA in 2027; EVP & CFO Early responded, "Yes, I think that's a fair assumption" and reiterated, "we said more than 70%."
  • Timothy Michael Moore, Clear Street: asked about interconnection moratorium timing and queues; CEO Bieber said interconnection times "take years" and are "a multiyear process typically" and noted interconnect "may be the last thing that happens."
  • Timothy Michael Moore, Clear Street: asked BESS revenue share; CEO Bieber said, "I don't have a number on that" and added, "I'm guessing it's in total, 5% or less right now."
  • Steven Wahrhaftig, Wedbush: asked about 2027 mix across commercial/utilities/government; CEO Bieber stated, "No, we're there already on a pro forma basis" and "for 2027, it will be about equal 1/3, 1/3, 1/3."
  • Steven Wahrhaftig, Wedbush: asked about the pace to get below 2.0x leverage; EVP & CFO Early said cash flow "is not consistent throughout the year" with "first quarter" weaker and "fourth quarter" strongest, adding, "it's possible that we reach that goal in the second quarter" but the company is "trying to be conservative."

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts’ tone was slightly negative to neutral on near-term uncertainty around data centers and deleveraging pace, reflected in questions about "data center permitting moratoriums and restrictions" and whether leverage targets were "pretty conservative" (Timothy Michael Moore, Clear Street; Steven Wahrhaftig, Wedbush).
  • Management tone was positive and confident on demand and pipeline, with CEO Bieber saying "demand for these data centers is not wavering" and "our pipeline goes out past 2029," while also showing some limitation on disclosed detail on BESS mix: "I don't have a number on that" (CEO Bieber).
  • Versus the prior quarter’s tone emphasizing acceleration and record margins (including "a record 28.2% adjusted EBITDA margin"), Q3 management messaging leaned more toward integrating Mantis financing and managing leverage, including "we will focus the majority of our strong free cash flow profile on debt reduction" (EVP & CFO Early, Q2 vs. Q3).

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • Strategic shift from signing/early integration (Burton) to closing and financing a larger deal: Q3 added "we closed the acquisition of Mantis Innovation" and detailed post-close capitalization including a "new $250 million term loan" and "net leverage of approximately 2.3x" pro forma (CEO Bieber; EVP & CFO Early).
  • Guidance language tightened upward again: Q3 raised 2026 targets to net revenue $435 million to $445 million, adjusted EBITDA $109 million to $111 million, and adjusted EPS $5.15 to $5.25, compared with Q2 targets of net revenue $415 million to $430 million, adjusted EBITDA $103 million to $107 million, and adjusted EPS $5.00 to $5.15 (EVP & CFO Early).
  • Profitability mix shifted quarter-to-quarter: Q3 adjusted EBITDA margin was "25.2%" vs. Q2 "28.2%"; Q2 management also cautioned that margin level would not hold, saying "we do not expect that margin to hold throughout the year" (EVP & CFO Early, Q2 vs. Q3).
  • Analyst focus rotated from LADWP ramp and tax treatment (Q2) to data center policy risk, Mantis cross-sell, and deleveraging timeline (Q3) (Q2 Q&A vs. Q3 Q&A).

Risks and Concerns

  • "Energy affordability" was framed as a central market constraint, as CEO Bieber said, "many specific locations in the grid have increased by more than 30%" and "Residential heating oil prices have increased 75% year-over-year," adding that "power affordability" has become "the most important consideration" for clients.
  • Integration and reporting risk around acquisition economics: management disclosed that under revised accounting guidelines, Mantis was expected to add "$75 million in net revenue, not the $120 million as previously communicated" (CEO Bieber).
  • Leverage and cash flow seasonality: management highlighted post-close leverage and timing variability, stating pro forma "net leverage" of "approximately 2.3x" and noting cash flow "is not consistent throughout the year" (EVP & CFO Early).

Final Takeaway

Management framed Q3 as another quarter of double-digit growth, highlighted the closing of Mantis and its expected $75 million net revenue contribution under updated guidelines, raised full-year 2026 targets again, and introduced preliminary 2027 targets calling for $1 billion contract revenue, more than $0.5 billion net revenue, and more than $140 million EBITDA, alongside a stated plan to use free cash flow for debt reduction toward a net leverage ratio below 2.0x by the end of Q3 2027.

data.title: Ring Energy outlines 2027 output of 21,000-23,000 boe/d with $135M-$165M capital plan as longer laterals expand
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Ring Energy (REI) Q3 2026

Management View

  • “During the quarter, we completed approximately $30.5 million of noncore asset sales, representing approximately 130 BOE per day, 63% of which was oil and approximately 9,800 net acres.” Quote (CEO & Chairman of the Board Paul McKinney). “We applied $10 million of those proceeds to reducing the borrowings under our revolving credit facility and approximately $18.8 million towards acquiring leasehold interest within and offsetting our existing Central Basin Platform operating footprint.” Quote (CEO & Chairman of the Board McKinney).
  • “Total sales volumes averaged 20,635 barrels of oil equivalent per day, up 3% from the second quarter, while oil sales volumes averaged 12,818 barrels of oil per day, up 1% sequentially.” Quote (CEO & Chairman of the Board McKinney). “We invested approximately $64 million to advance our co-developed longer lateral program and supporting infrastructure… As a result, our adjusted free cash flow was negative during the third quarter.” Quote (CEO & Chairman of the Board McKinney).
  • “Let me be clear about this. We have not lost focus on maximizing adjusted free cash flow, strengthening our balance sheet and lowering our leverage ratio.” Quote (CEO & Chairman of the Board McKinney). “With the capital spending stepping down in the fourth quarter, we expect to return to positive free cash flow and remain positive for the full year.” Quote (CEO & Chairman of the Board McKinney).
  • “Revenue was $102.3 million, down just 2% from the second quarter despite a 12% decline in our realized oil price.” Quote (Executive VP, CFO, Principal Financial Officer & Treasurer Sundip Johl). “Our net realized natural gas price was negative $0.30 per Mcf compared with a negative $5.20 per Mcf in the second quarter.” Quote (Executive VP, CFO, Principal Financial Officer & Treasurer Johl).

Outlook

  • “For the fourth quarter of 2026, adjusted for the asset divestitures, we expect oil sales volumes to be between 12,900 and 13,500 barrels per day and total sales volumes of 20,400 to 21,200 barrels of oil equivalent per day.” Quote (CEO & Chairman of the Board McKinney). “We expect fourth quarter LOE of $9.80 to $10.30 per BOE and capital spending of approximately $43 million to $48 million.” Quote (CEO & Chairman of the Board McKinney).
  • “Looking further ahead to 2027, we expect oil sales volumes to be 13,200 to 14,300 barrels per day and total sales volumes of 21,000 to 23,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day.” Quote (CEO & Chairman of the Board McKinney). “Our preliminary capital range of $135 million to $165 million, including 20 to 30 new horizontal wells with laterals longer than 1.5 miles.” Quote (CEO & Chairman of the Board McKinney).
  • “We recently strengthened our oil hedge position by increasing the level of downside protection on a portion of our existing hedged volumes… Based on the midpoint of our full year 2027 oil sales guidance, approximately 59% of our first half 2027 oil volumes are currently hedged.” Quote (Executive VP, CFO, Principal Financial Officer & Treasurer Johl). “The impact becomes meaningful in a lower price environment… designed to help ensure we remain free cash flow positive even at $65 WTI.” Quote (Executive VP, CFO, Principal Financial Officer & Treasurer Johl).

Financial Results

  • “Adjusted EBITDA increased approximately 5% sequentially to $57.1 million, with adjusted EBITDA margin improving to 56% from 52%, while adjusted cash flow from operations increased approximately 7% to $50.4 million.” Quote (Executive VP, CFO, Principal Financial Officer & Treasurer Johl).
  • “LOE was $10.20 per BOE compared with $10.12 in the second quarter… all-in cash operating costs declined to $21.03 per BOE from $21.59 in the second quarter.” Quote (Executive VP, CFO, Principal Financial Officer & Treasurer Johl). “Interest expense also continued to move lower, declining to $7.7 million from $8.4 million in the second quarter, reflecting lower debt balances.” Quote (Executive VP, CFO, Principal Financial Officer & Treasurer Johl).
  • “We ended September with $350 million outstanding under our revolving credit facility, down $10 million from the end of the second quarter and $70 million from the beginning of the year.” Quote (Executive VP, CFO, Principal Financial Officer & Treasurer Johl). “Our leverage ratio… improved to approximately 1.5x from 1.7x last quarter.” Quote (Executive VP, CFO, Principal Financial Officer & Treasurer Johl).

Q&A

  • Jeffrey Robertson, Water Tower Research LLC: “For 2027… can you share your perspective on the metrics with respect to how much production Ring would expect to add as you… pivot to 1.5-mile horizontals or 2-mile horizontals…?” CEO McKinney: “we believe… switching… to longer laterals, co-developing our locations… delivers significantly more production per dollar spent,” and “we… guided, 10% production growth next year on a very similar and actually slightly lower capital spending program.”
  • Jeffrey Robertson, Water Tower Research LLC: “when you co-develop wells on pads, are you… shutting in offset production…?” CEO McKinney: “in most instances, we will be shutting in production offsetting because… we’re trying to minimize the frac interference,” adding “you’re going to see higher sustained production delivery” and “considerably more production per dollar spend as we go into 2027.”
  • Jeffrey Robertson, Water Tower Research LLC: “what’s informing your view of what kind of capital activity you might want in the second half of 2027…?” CEO McKinney: “we front-loaded our capital for 2027… We may curtail our capital spending and we may increase capital spending all based on cash flow,” and “we really want to get below 1.25x, but I really want it below 1x.”
  • Noel Parks, Tuohy Brothers Investment Research, Inc.: “how you sort of rate the acreage that you have… how you’re selecting, what you’re willing to sell…?” CEO McKinney: “it became very apparent to us that these assets that we had were more valuable in the hands of somebody else,” and “those prices… are very attractive, very accretive.”
  • Noel Parks, Tuohy Brothers Investment Research, Inc.: asked for color on recent drilling encouragement; CEO McKinney: “we’re not going to talk about specific well performance right now, primarily because… we’re still acquiring acreage.” COO Alexander Dyes: “the big confidence… is by updating our guidance showing that we are going to grow more than we have in previous years,” and “previously, we had 2 proved horizontal targets, while now we proved up to 5 horizontal targets.”
  • Noel Parks, Tuohy Brothers Investment Research, Inc.: asked what is driving confidence; EVP & Chief Exploration Officer James Parr: “we’re getting encouragement in all of the zones that we’re drilling… Some of them are exceeding our expectations,” and “the geology is all excellent.” CEO McKinney added that “what was previously believed to be uneconomic… now this new emerging technology… we’re finding” can work economically.
  • Jeffrey Robertson, Water Tower Research LLC: “how does the decreasing leverage ratio affect the hedge requirements under the RBL?” CFO Johl: “we’re still on that rolling 24-month basis,” and timing “really depends on the pricing environment.” CEO McKinney: “you got to be below 1.25x and you have to be at least 50% or less drawn on your borrowing base” to reduce requirements, and “if you can get it below 25% drawn… then you don’t have any hedging requirements on months 13 through 24.”

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analyst tone was neutral and detail-oriented, pressing on capital efficiency, production lumpiness, and hedge constraints, including questions like “are you… shutting in offset production…?” (Jeffrey Robertson, Water Tower Research LLC) and “how does the decreasing leverage ratio affect the hedge requirements under the RBL?” (Jeffrey Robertson, Water Tower Research LLC).
  • Management tone was slightly positive but included clear boundary-setting and caution on near-term visibility: “Let me be clear about this,” (CEO & Chairman of the Board McKinney) and “we’re not going to talk about specific well performance right now” (CEO & Chairman of the Board McKinney).
  • Compared with Q2’s heavier macro framing (“My view remains that the current market continues to underestimate…” Quote (CEO & Chairman of the Board Paul McKinney)), Q3 leaned more on execution and program mechanics, including “this was a deliberate decision” on spending (CEO & Chairman of the Board McKinney) and “The third quarter was a deliberate investment quarter” (Executive VP, CFO, Principal Financial Officer & Treasurer Johl).

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • In Q3, management reported completed divestitures and reinvestment (“completed approximately $30.5 million of noncore asset sales” Quote (CEO & Chairman of the Board McKinney)), while Q2 emphasized that the company was “continuing to evaluate select non-core assets” Quote (CEO & Chairman of the Board Paul McKinney).
  • Guidance framing shifted from Q2’s second-half 2026 ranges (“For the second half of ’26, we now expect oil sales volumes to range…” Quote (CEO & Chairman of the Board Paul McKinney)) to Q3’s explicit Q4 2026 outlook “adjusted for the asset divestitures” and a reiterated preliminary 2027 capital band of $135 million to $165 million (CEO & Chairman of the Board McKinney).
  • Hedging emphasis evolved from Q2’s description of substantial 2026 hedge coverage (CFO Johl discussed “approximately 1.7 million barrels of oil hedged… approximately 70%” Quote (Executive VP, CFO, Principal Financial Officer & Treasurer Sundip Johl)) to Q3’s focus on strengthening downside protection and targeting free cash flow resilience “even at $65 WTI” Quote (Executive VP, CFO, Principal Financial Officer & Treasurer Johl).

Risks and Concerns

  • “You’re going to see is going to be a little bit more lumpy” as the company moves to multi-well co-developed pads, and “in most instances, we will be shutting in production” during completions. Quote (CEO & Chairman of the Board McKinney). Management described the mitigation as better multi-quarter outcomes: “on a multiple quarter basis, you’re going to see higher sustained production delivery.” Quote (CEO & Chairman of the Board McKinney).
  • Management highlighted commodity-price sensitivity in leverage and covenant flexibility: “it really depends on the pricing environment we’re at and how quickly we can get to that leverage ratio.” Quote (Executive VP, CFO, Principal Financial Officer & Treasurer Johl). The mitigation discussed was added hedge protection concentrated in early 2027 (“approximately 59% of our first half 2027 oil volumes are currently hedged” Quote (Executive VP, CFO, Principal Financial Officer & Treasurer Johl)).
  • Management flagged competitive dynamics around leasing as a reason for withholding well-level disclosure: “we’re still acquiring acreage… we just don’t want to drive up the competition.” Quote (CEO & Chairman of the Board McKinney).

Final Takeaway

Ring’s management described Q3 2026 as “a deliberate investment quarter” (Executive VP, CFO, Principal Financial Officer & Treasurer Johl), pairing $30.5 million of divestitures with accelerated spending on longer laterals and infrastructure, while still reducing revolver borrowings and lowering leverage. The company’s stated near-term setup is for lower Q4 capital and a return to positive free cash flow, alongside a 2027 plan calling for 21,000 to 23,000 BOE/d and $135 million to $165 million of capital, with hedges and balance-sheet targets positioned as key enablers of the program.

data.title: Carlyle Secured Lending outlines plan to ramp SCP to $6B to $7B of assets while targeting 4 CLOs per year
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Carlyle Secured Lending Inc. (CGBD) Q3 2026

Management View

  • "During the third quarter, macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainty weighed on direct lending volume, which declined year-over-year as private equity activity remains slower than anticipated." (CEO Alex Chi) "In total, excluding joint venture activity, we funded $81 million of investments at CGBD." (CEO Chi)
  • "On our new originations, weighted average spreads on those deals were approximately 505 basis points... and our weighted average leverage on entry continued to decrease by over 2/3 of a turn quarter-over-quarter to 4.9x, with a substantial majority of the deals in the quarter having financial maintenance covenants." (CEO Chi)
  • "Both of our JVs, MMCF and SCP, continue to scale and generate attractive returns to CGBD." (CEO Chi) "At SCP, the portfolio grew to $2.1 billion and produced an annualized dividend yield of 20.3% to CGBD." (CEO Chi)
  • "In line with the revised dividend policy, our Board of Directors declared a fourth quarter 2026 dividend of $0.35 per share, which is fully covered by net investment income." (CEO Chi) "Our net asset value as of September 30 increased to $15.65 per share, up from $15.61 per share as of June 30." (CEO Chi)
  • "Total investment income for the third quarter was $63 million, up from $62 million last quarter... [and] total expenses of $38 million were in line with prior quarter." (President and CFO Thomas Hennigan) "The result was net investment income for the third quarter of $25 million or $0.36 per share." (CFO Hennigan)

Outlook

  • "With 0.25 point Federal Reserve hike in September... we expect rising rates to be an earnings tailwind as nearly 100% of our portfolio is floating rate." (CEO Alex Chi)
  • "From an underwriting perspective, Carlyle continues to take a measured approach to data center and GPU financing transactions... we have minimal exposure to compute infrastructure and remain selective." (CEO Chi)
  • "We still anticipate achieving full dividend coverage in future quarters, along with an increase in earnings and supplemental dividends as we continue to ramp the JVs and benefit from increasing rates based on the latest forward curve." (President and CFO Thomas Hennigan)
  • "We expect the more normalized yield to be mid-teens longer term." (CFO Hennigan)

Financial Results

  • "Total investment income for the third quarter was $63 million... primarily driven by an increase in dividend income from both the MMCF and SCP JVs." (President and CFO Thomas Hennigan) "The result was net investment income for the third quarter of $25 million or $0.36 per share." (CFO Hennigan)

Q&A

  • Erik Zwick, Lucid Capital Markets, LLC: Asked about "growth in derivatives liabilities"; President and CFO Hennigan said, "That is our interest rate swaps for our bonds... it's just an offset based on interest rates going up." (CFO Hennigan)

(CEO Chi)

  • Robert Dodd, Raymond James & Associates, Inc.: Asked for an aerospace/defense concentration cap; CEO Chi said, "we are absolutely focused on diversification" and added, "Not going to go out with a specific hard cap on the sector." (CEO Chi)

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • Platform activity at CGBD shifted from "funded $248 million of investments" in Q2 (CEO Alex Chi) to "funded $81 million of investments" in Q3 (CEO Chi), with Q3 explicitly citing "direct lending volume... declined year-over-year" (CEO Chi).
  • Credit marks improved from "realized and unrealized net loss... about $24 million, or $0.35 per share" in Q2 (President and CFO Thomas Hennigan) to "about $1 million or $0.02 per share" in Q3 (CFO Hennigan).
  • Nonaccruals rose from "only 0.6%... at fair value" in Q2 (CFO Hennigan) to "1.1% of investments at fair value" in Q3 (CFO Hennigan).
  • Analyst focus rotated from Q2 questions emphasizing deal market pricing and fees (Richard Shane, JPMorgan; Justin for Lucid) to Q3 questions emphasizing balance-sheet hedges, buyback vs. deployment, and SCP dividend accounting (Erik Zwick; Robert Dodd).

Risks and Concerns

  • "Macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainty" and "private equity activity remains slower than anticipated" were cited as headwinds for volume. (CEO Alex Chi)
  • "The markets continue to experience volatility related to the anticipated quantum of future debt issuance needed to finance the AI compute build-out," and management said it is taking "a measured approach" with "minimal exposure to compute infrastructure." (CEO Chi)
  • On portfolio stress, management reported, "We did add 2 positions to nonaccrual in the quarter" and said, "We continue to work closely with these sponsors and borrowers." (President and CFO Thomas Hennigan)

Final Takeaway

Management emphasized lower near-term origination volumes alongside steady portfolio positioning, stating that Q4 activity could remain "muted" while the current pipeline supports "more optimism" into early 2027. The quarter featured $0.36 per share of net investment income with a $0.35 base dividend declared for Q4, modest share repurchases, and relatively flat aggregate valuations, while nonaccruals increased to 1.1% of fair value. Management continued to highlight joint venture scaling—particularly SCP’s CLO issuance cadence and a longer-term mid-teens normalized yield—while maintaining caution on AI-related credit market looseness and emphasizing selectivity and diversification.

data.title: Dauch projects $10.8B-$10.875B sales in 2026 while integration synergies reach $100M run rate
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Dauch Corporation (DCH) Q3 2026

Management View

  • "Despite production volatility and rising input costs, we generated strong cash flow in the quarter while supporting new program launches," said Chairman & CEO David Dauch, adding that "we are making excellent progress on our synergy realization" and that "9 months into the combination, it is increasingly clear that we have created a stronger company." (Chairman & CEO David Dauch)
  • "The company's third quarter 2026 sales were approximately $2.9 billion and adjusted earnings per share was $0.22 per share, and adjusted free cash flow was approximately $127 million," with Q3 dynamics including "good performance on key GM crossover and Land Rover utility vehicle programs" but "lower Ram Heavy Duty volumes," plus "major launch activity underway at GM for its large pickup truck program with planned downtime." (Chairman & CEO Dauch)
  • "We have already realized $100 million of run rate synergies and savings to date" and management said it will "clearly deliver on our goal or more than $100 million of run rate synergies by year-end," citing progress in "optimizing our SG&A" and capturing "global engineering efficiencies." (Chairman & CEO Dauch)
  • Management highlighted two Q3 wins: "the next-generation business for propshafts, sideshafts and electronic limited slip differentials on a premier European luxury SUV program" expected "deep into the 2030" and "sideshaft content for an infantry squad vehicle program" as an entry into adjacent markets. (Chairman & CEO Dauch)
  • "In the third quarter of 2026, our sales were $2.91 billion" and "adjusted EBITDA was $358.5 million and adjusted EBITDA margin was 12.3%," while "we grew our realized synergy benefit momentum with a positive $25 million in savings." (Executive VP & CFO Chris May)

Outlook

  • "Sales now in the range of $10.8 billion to $10.875 billion, adjusted EBITDA in the range of $1.35 billion to $1.375 billion and adjusted free cash flow of approximately $270 million to $310 million," management said, describing the update as reflecting near-term headwinds but continued integration progress. (Chairman & CEO Dauch)
  • Management described the EBITDA outlook change as reflecting "increasing inflationary pressures, particularly stemming from higher fuel and energy costs," "a somewhat elevated Tier 2 and Tier 3 supplier stress level" and "pockets of some production volatility stemming from customer schedule adjustments." (Executive VP & CFO May)
  • The company said the sales outlook was "raised and tightened" to $10.8 billion to $10.875 billion "versus $10.6 billion to $10.8 billion previously" and that it anticipates GM full-size pickup and SUV production of "approximately 1.4 million units" in 2026. (Executive VP & CFO May)
  • For modeling, management said: "please continue to use approximately 245 million shares for the fourth quarter for modeling purposes" and added, "as for 2027, we would expect to provide our official outlook when we announce our fourth quarter earnings call next February." (Executive VP & CFO May)

Financial Results

  • Management reported a Q3 profitability bridge that included legacy and acquired operations: "adjusted EBITDA for legacy Dauch was $193 million" and "Legacy Dowlais contributed approximately $140 million of adjusted EBITDA," while year-over-year comparisons reflected that Dowlais had "approximately $30 million from onetime commercial settlements" in 2025. (Executive VP & CFO May)
  • Balance sheet and interest costs were framed as acquisition-related: "Net interest expense was $80.9 million" and the "weighted average interest rate of our outstanding long-term debt was approximately 7.1%," while the company ended Q3 with "net debt of approximately $4.1 billion and net leverage ratio of 2.6x." (Executive VP & CFO May)
  • On earnings, management said: "our GAAP net loss was $45.3 million or $0.19 per share" and "Adjusted earnings per share... was $0.22 per share." (Executive VP & CFO May)
  • Cash and liquidity items included: "Net cash provided by operating activities... was $150.1 million," "Capital expenditures... were $94.7 million," and "we now have no significant debt maturities until 2029" after redeeming "the remaining $125 million of our 2028 notes." (Executive VP & CFO May)

Q&A

  • Gautam Narayan, RBC Capital Markets: "how should we think about these incremental headwinds bleeding into 2027?" Chris May: "in Q4, we have generally 4 or 5 less production days... I would expect probably an impact... of around $10 million" from inflationary pressures and said pressures "would probably continue into the early part of next year" while actions include "self-help" and customer discussions that "take time to play out." (Executive VP May)
  • Gautam Narayan, RBC Capital Markets: asked what offsets a CapEx cut within the guide; Chris May: "Our cash taxes are up slightly" and "working capital timing would be the remaining difference," plus "final billings that came in with our acquisition." (Executive VP May)
  • Joseph Spak, UBS: asked about mark-to-market items; Chris May: "that does not impact our adjusted EBITDA... It is noncash in nature" and described "nondesignated dollar derivatives" that "will burn out relatively quickly." (Executive VP May)
  • Joseph Spak, UBS: asked about deleveraging approach; David Dauch: "we want to work our way under 2x" and said the acquisition was intended "to accelerate that cash generation opportunity through the synergies." (Chairman & CEO Dauch)
  • James Mulholland, Deutsche Bank: asked if faster synergies imply upside; David Dauch: "we have been very aggressive" on "SG&A cost as well as engineering efficiencies" and said "we think there's more opportunity here and hold tight for future discussions." (Chairman & CEO Dauch)
  • Dan Levy, Barclays: asked how inflation is handled; Chris May: customer recoveries in 2022 "took ultimately the better part of the year" and current actions include optimizing "freight routes" and alternatives for "coolants," with a "very similar path" expected. (Executive VP May)
  • Yash Beswala, JPMorgan: asked about defense adjacency and pipeline; David Dauch: aerospace and defense "would be one of those markets" and on quoting said, "we're still quoting approximately that $2 billion" and referenced a "25% to 30% hit rate." (Chairman & CEO Dauch)
  • Andrew Percoco, Morgan Stanley: asked about the GM changeover; David Dauch: "Everything is on track and on schedule" and Chris May added: "our content per vehicle, our margin profile very similar" between generations. (Chairman & CEO Dauch; Executive VP May)
  • Douglas Karson, BofA Securities: asked about tariffs; Chris May: "we are still impacted around $20 million to $25 million from a bottom line perspective in calendar year 2026." (Executive VP May)

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts’ tone was slightly negative to neutral, pressing on Q4 implied downshift, inflation pass-through, supplier stress, and Europe/China exposure (e.g., RBC called out "a sizable downshift" and asked how much bleeds into 2027).
  • Management tone was slightly positive in prepared remarks but more measured in Q&A, repeatedly emphasizing mitigation timing and uncertainty while asserting execution confidence, including "we are confident in our ability to navigate these challenges" and that inflation discussions "take time to play out." (Chairman & CEO Dauch; Executive VP May)
  • Versus last quarter, management language shifted from Q2’s "excellent second quarter" and limited operational impact from energy prices to Q3’s emphasis on "additional inflationary pressures" and "Tier 2 and Tier 3 supplier stress level" as explicit headwinds. (Chairman & CEO Dauch; Executive VP May)

Quarter-over-quarter Comparison

  • Q3 reported "sales were approximately $2.9 billion" vs. Q2 "sales were approximately $3 billion," and Q3 adjusted EPS of "$0.22" vs. Q2 "$0.32," alongside Q3 commentary about "production volatility" versus Q2’s view that production was "stable." (Chairman & CEO Dauch)
  • Guidance language moved from Q2 lifting the low end to Q3 "raised and tightened" sales but lowered the EBITDA range midpoint, with Q3 attributing the change to energy-driven inflation and supplier stress. (Executive VP May)
  • Synergy progress advanced from Q2 "approximately $70 million of run rate savings" to Q3 "$100 million of run rate synergies and savings to date," with Q3 stating year-1 run-rate target is already achieved within three quarters post-combination. (Chairman & CEO Dauch)
  • Analyst focus widened from Q2 emphasis on cash restructuring cadence and USMCA to Q3 emphasis on inflation, supplier health, and regional competitive pressure (including Europe and Chinese OEM penetration). (Multiple analysts)

Risks and Concerns

  • Management flagged that it "began to experience additional inflationary pressures across the supply chain" and that "supply chain challenges are beginning to become more apparent, especially with some of the Tier 2 and Tier 3 suppliers," with mitigation described as "flexing our variable cost structure, driving productivity and optimizing our operations" and pursuing customer "compensation." (Chairman & CEO Dauch; Executive VP May)
  • The company highlighted customer-driven volatility: "planned downtime" tied to GM’s large pickup transition and weaker "Ram Heavy Duty volumes," and added that tariffs remain a bottom-line headwind of "$20 million to $25 million" in 2026. (Chairman & CEO Dauch; Executive VP May)

Final Takeaway

Management framed Q3 as a cash-generative quarter amid production volatility, with integration and synergy execution ahead of schedule at a $100 million run-rate level. The company updated full-year 2026 guidance to $10.8 billion-$10.875 billion of sales, $1.35 billion-$1.375 billion of adjusted EBITDA, and $270 million-$310 million of adjusted free cash flow, while describing inflation (fuel/energy), Tier 2/Tier 3 supplier stress, and customer schedule adjustments as the primary near-term pressure points. The call also emphasized continued deleveraging intent, including a stated goal to get "under 2x," and highlighted new program wins spanning both core driveline content and adjacent defense-related applications.

data.title: Iamgold outlines ~$150/oz Côté cash cost reduction starting 2027 as it plans to repurchase 50% of Franco-Nevada royalty for ~$525M
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: IAMGOLD Corporation (IMG:CA) Q3 2026

Management View

  • "The third quarter was another safe and steady quarter for IAMGOLD." (CEO, President & Director Renaud Adams) "We produced 186,900 attributable ounces, bringing year-to-date production to 558,600 ounces." (CEO Adams) "We are on track to meet full year guidance and expect the fourth quarter to be our strongest led by Côté." (CEO Adams)
  • "Yesterday, we notified Franco-Nevada that we are exercising our right to repurchase half of its gross margin royalty on Côté for approximately $525 million." (CEO Adams) "IAMGOLD will fund the full amount and keep the full benefit, lowering Côté's cash costs, including royalties, by roughly $150 an ounce starting in 2027." (CEO Adams)
  • "Operationally, the third quarter was a turning point at Côté." (CEO Adams) "In September, the plant averaged 37,100 tonnes per day, above nameplate, and processing costs fell to $15.36 per tonne." (CEO Adams)
  • "Mine site free cash flow was $404.3 million in the quarter, bringing year-to-date mine site free cash flow to $1.3 billion." (Chief Financial Officer Marthinus Theunissen) "Revenue for the third quarter was $856.5 million from sales of 199,900 ounces at an average realized gold price of $4,277 per ounce." (CFO Theunissen)
  • "Côté produced 92,000 ounces on a 100% basis in the third quarter or 64,400 ounces to our account." (Chief Operating Officer Bruno Lemelin) "The plant averaged 37,100 tonnes per day... above nameplate of 36,000 tonnes per day." (COO Lemelin) "We plan to exit 2026 at about $4 per tonne for mining and about $15 per tonne for milling." (COO Lemelin)

Outlook

  • "We are on track to meet full year guidance." (CEO Adams) "We need about 161,000 attributable ounces in the fourth quarter to reach the low end of our consolidated guidance." (CEO Adams)
  • "Our full year total capital expenditure guidance of $500 million, plus or minus 5%, is unchanged, which implies a step-up in spending in the fourth quarter." (CFO Theunissen) "Within that total, we have reduced sustaining capital at Côté to $130 million... from $160 million... [and] increased... at Essakane to $165 million from $105 million." (CFO Theunissen)
  • "We expect the transaction to close in December with economic effect from January 1, 2027." (CFO Theunissen) "[It] reduc[es] our effective gross margin royalty from 7.5% to 2.14%." (CFO Theunissen)
  • "We remain on track to release the updated Côté mine plan and mineral reserve estimate this quarter... [and] set out a near-term path to take the plant from 36,000 tonnes per day to 40,000 tonnes per day." (COO Lemelin) "We expect to publish a preliminary economic assessment for the [Nelligan] complex in mid-2027." (CEO Adams)

Financial Results

  • "Mine site free cash flow was $404.3 million in the quarter" and "Operating cash flow before working capital and taxes for the first 9 months was $1.7 billion." (CFO Theunissen)
  • "At September 30, IAMGOLD had $766.6 million in cash and cash equivalents with our $850 million credit facility undrawn for total liquidity of approximately $1.6 billion." (CFO Theunissen) "Our only remaining debt is the $450 million of senior notes due October 2028, redeemable at par since October 15." (CFO Theunissen)
  • "Adjusted EBITDA in the third quarter was $503.9 million." (CFO Theunissen) "Adjusted net earnings attributable to equity holders were $237 million or $0.42 per share compared with $170.9 million or $0.30 per share in the prior period." (CFO Theunissen)
  • "During the third quarter, we repurchased and canceled approximately 7.6 million shares for $134.7 million" and "Since the program began... we have repurchased 32.1 million shares for $592.6 million." (CFO Theunissen) "Subsequent to quarter end, our Board authorized the company to seek TSX approval for a new normal course issuer bid... for up to approximately 10% of our outstanding shares." (CFO Theunissen)

Q&A

  • Anita Soni, CIBC Capital Markets: asked if Côté could sustain the "$15-ish" per tonne processing cost into Q4/2027 and about mining-cost drivers; COO Lemelin: "Yes, that's the plan" and "No major shutdown until the end of the year and for 2027," adding mining-cost actions including "rely less on rehandling" and targeting "towards the $4 and even like... the mid-$3s later on"; she also asked about modeling the post-buyback royalty; CFO Theunissen: "It would be revenue less cash cost, so your gross margin times the 2.14%."
  • Fahad Tariq, Jefferies: asked whether the $525 million royalty buyback would be funded with cash vs. debt and about payback/IRR plus study assumptions; CFO Theunissen: "we will be using cash from the balance sheet" and "If there is a need, we may have to draw on the credit facility, but it would be very short term"; CEO Adams: "We're going to use $2,100 an ounce for the reserve price for the study" and said the study is "the new base case" and "does not highlight beyond" the 40,000 tonnes per day path.
  • Mohamed Sidibe, National Bank Financial: asked about Burkina local refining order and cash repatriation; CEO Adams: "There is no date on the exemption" and "business as usual for the time being"; CFO Theunissen: delays could create "working capital" impacts but "it doesn't affect our ability to repatriate cash"; Sidibe also asked about Westwood sludge timing; CFO Theunissen: "processing has just started this week" and expects "over the course of November and first half of December" to finish assays and convert to sales.
  • Harrison Reynolds, RBC Capital Markets: asked about sludge payability and recurrence; COO Lemelin: "we have modified our standard operating procedures" and will manage potential future material "on a monthly basis"; CEO Adams: "we do not feel that there's been loss of gold over those years" and "moving forward, you should not expect any adjustment"; CFO Theunissen (on payability): "Mid to very high 90%." Reynolds also asked about October Côté trends; CEO Adams: "the tendency and the rhythm has continued in October."
  • Delvin Xie, Scotiabank: asked about Q4 production strength and unit-cost direction and 2027 inflation, hedging, and Nelligan PEA cutoff; CEO Adams: "we remain very, very confident" on guidance and "we think that we could achieve towards $15 for the full quarter" at Côté; CFO Theunissen: inflation assumption "3% to 4%... excluding the impact of diesel" and said the company is "look[ing] at putting in additional gold hedges at Côté"; CEO Adams on PEA drill cutoff: "at year-end, correct."
  • Medina Abdullina, Freedom Broker: asked about stripping/sustaining capital carryover and Westwood underground cost normalization; CFO Theunissen: Essakane 2027 capex "would be slightly higher" to advance "Block 3 and mine life extension"; CEO Adams: "you should expect '27 to be somewhat in the range of '26" at Westwood.
  • Anita Soni, CIBC Capital Markets (follow-up): asked about Côté/Gosselin conversion and sequencing plus Burkina refining exemption/cost; CEO Adams: "we continue to be very confident that we could convert that to 70% plus" and reiterated on refining "There is no date" and the focus is "making sure we don't create further delays."

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts: slightly negative to neutral, with repeated requests for durability and mechanics of cost/royalty benefits and jurisdiction/process risk, including "Would that be sustained into Q4 and 2027?" (Anita Soni, CIBC) and "has this requirement impacted... cash repatriation" (Mohamed Sidibe, National Bank Financial).
  • Management: slightly positive in prepared remarks and neutral-to-slightly positive in Q&A, emphasizing execution and visibility, including "we remain very, very confident to hit" guidance (CEO Adams) and "Yes, that's the plan" on sustaining performance (COO Lemelin), while limiting specifics on sensitive items ("it's commercially sensitive information" on payability rates (CFO Theunissen)).
  • Versus the prior quarter, management language shifted from evaluating the Franco-Nevada option ("we continue to look at buyback opportunity" (CFO Theunissen, Q2)) to committing to execute it ("we are exercising our right" (CEO Adams, Q3)), while analyst tone remained focused on Côté ramp and capital allocation.

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • Capital allocation shifted from optionality to action on the Côté royalty: "we continue to look at buyback opportunity of that royalty" (CFO Theunissen, Q2) versus "we are exercising our right to repurchase half" (CEO Adams, Q3) and "we expect the transaction to close in December" (CFO Theunissen, Q3).
  • Côté operating narrative moved from early benefits after contractor crushing ended ("processing cost in June averaged $17.72 per tonne" (COO Lemelin, Q2)) to a September datapoint at or near target ("processing costs fell to $15.36 per tonne" (CEO Adams, Q3)) and a stated exit objective ("exit 2026 at about $15 per tonne for milling" (COO Lemelin, Q3)).
  • Liquidity increased quarter-to-quarter: "$501.4 million in cash... total available liquidity of approximately $1.35 billion" (CFO Theunissen, Q2) versus "$766.6 million in cash... total liquidity of approximately $1.6 billion" (CFO Theunissen, Q3).
  • Study cadence language tightened: Q2 framed Côté technical report "towards the end of the year" (CEO Adams, Q2), while Q3 said the updated plan will be released "this quarter" and will "combine Côté and Gosselin for the first time" (CEO Adams, Q3).

Risks and Concerns

  • "Both Côté and Essakane carry royalties that are directly linked to the gold price" and with a higher realized gold price, "royalties have averaged $370 per ounce this year." (CEO Adams)
  • Energy sensitivity remained explicit: "a $10 per barrel move in oil represents about $12 per ounce on our consolidated costs." (CEO Adams)
  • Burkina refining decree risk was framed as process timing: "the real risk... is really working capital and if it delays the gold sales process" (CFO Theunissen), with mitigation described as "very good alignment with the government" (CFO Theunissen) and a "temporary exemption" (COO Lemelin).
  • Westwood sludge uncertainty was repeatedly emphasized: "this is not an estimate of recoverable or payable gold" and "Any gold recovered... is not included in our 2026 guidance." (COO Lemelin)

Final Takeaway

Management framed Q3 as setting up a stronger Q4 led by Côté, while highlighting balance sheet capacity and capital returns alongside a major capital allocation decision: a ~$525 million repurchase of half the Franco-Nevada Côté gross margin royalty, intended to lower Côté cash costs by roughly $150/oz starting in 2027. Executives tied near-term operating focus to sustaining nameplate throughput and cost targets at Côté, continued cash generation at Essakane to fund buybacks, and multiple upcoming catalysts including the combined Côté-Gosselin mine plan (using a $2,100/oz reserve price assumption) and a mid-2027 PEA for the Nelligan Mining Complex.

data.title: Brookfield targets infrastructure flagship to exceed $30B in early 2027 as net carry is expected to total ~$3B in 2029-2031
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Brookfield Asset Management (BAM) Q3 2026

Management View

  • "We raised $123 billion in the first 3 quarters of the year, including $25 billion of capital in the third quarter." (Chief Executive Officer Connor David Teskey)
  • "Fee-bearing capital reached $682 billion, up 13% over the last 12 months, which drove third quarter fee-related earnings to $864 million or $0.54 per share and distributable earnings to $763 million or $0.47 per share." (CEO Teskey)
  • "Carried interest realizations have begun earlier than projected and will continue to scale, adding a new source of growth on top of that growing and durable base." (CEO Teskey)
  • "The fund has received commitments of $26 billion to date, including $13 billion subsequent to the end of the quarter... This puts us well on track to exceed our $30 billion target in early 2027." (Managing Partner of Infrastructure Rene Lubianski)
  • "In the past 2 weeks, we have announced 2 new investments. In Korea, we agreed to provide approximately $9 billion of capital alongside NAVER and NVIDIA to deploy 200 megawatts of AI computing capacity." (Managing Partner Lubianski)
  • "In the United Kingdom, we announced a partnership with Drax to develop up to 1 gigawatt scale AI factory at a Drax power station site with the potential for more than GBP 20 billion of investment over time." (Managing Partner Lubianski)
  • "We delivered another strong quarter with double-digit growth in both fee-related and distributable earnings." (CFO & Managing Partner of Infrastructure Hadley Marshall)

Outlook

  • "We continue to expect a record year for fundraising, along with record deployment and strong monetization activity that is built throughout the year." (CFO Marshall)
  • "We also expect earnings in line with our long-term targets though modestly below what we expected at the beginning of the year due to 2 factors." (CFO Marshall)
  • "We'll begin charging fees in the fund as of January 1, a couple of months later than initially planned as we complete deployment of the prior vintage." (CFO Marshall)
  • "With the share price down this year, we no longer expect to earn that fee in 2026." (CFO Marshall, on BBU performance fee)
  • "That fee is deferred, not lost, and remains available to us on equal terms as BBU's price recovers." (CFO Marshall)

Financial Results

  • "Fee-related earnings, or FRE, in the quarter increased 15% from the prior year period to $864 million or $0.54 per share." (CFO Marshall)
  • "Distributable earnings, or DE, were $763 million or $0.47 per share in the quarter, also up 15% from the prior year period, bringing DE over the last 12 months to $2.9 billion." (CFO Marshall)
  • "This quarter marked an important milestone for Brookfield... resulting in $48 million of net realized carry to BAM." (CFO Marshall)
  • "If our funds hit their targets, it would mean that we will realize a total of approximately $3 billion of net carry between 2029 and 2031... averaging more than $2 billion of net realized carry per year from 2032 through 2037." (CFO Marshall)
  • "We invested or committed approximately $36 billion and generated approximately $12 billion of equity proceeds from monetizations in the quarter." (CFO Marshall)
  • "We have $148 billion of uncalled fund commitments, including $68 billion that is not currently earning fees and expected to generate approximately $680 million of additional annual revenues as it is deployed." (CFO Marshall)
  • "We ended the quarter with $2.1 billion of corporate liquidity following the completion of Oaktree acquisition." (CFO Marshall)

Q&A

  • Cherilyn Radbourne, TD Cowen: Asked whether Brookfield’s partnership approach helps AI factory execution and what must be in place before deploying capital; Chief Executive Officer Teskey: "We look to derisk the development, only putting capital in the ground once we've secured offtake equipment supply and permits. We only build in places where we have long-term community support."
  • Craig Siegenthaler, BofA Securities: Asked how AI fits Brookfield’s historically contrarian/value approach and downside risks like construction delays and power; CEO Teskey: "We are treating AI infrastructure the exact same way we treat all other types of infrastructure... focusing on the largest projects with the best counterparties at a scale that few can operate."
  • Bart Dziarski, RBC Capital Markets: Asked for fundraising building blocks for 2027 and the role of countercyclical strategies; CEO Teskey: "Today, we view that baseline as north of $100 billion regardless of what products are in the market" and "we do expect both our real estate and our Oaktree opportunistic credit fund to launch next year."
  • Alexander Blostein, Goldman Sachs: Asked how much AI investment is insulated from permitting/regulatory risk vs. in-flight projects; CEO Teskey: "We don't put dollars in the ground until the permits are secured... the amount of... speculative development dollars... would be... de minimis."
  • Kenneth Worthington, JPMorgan: Asked for the multiyear outlook for credit growth; CEO Teskey: "We view in our plans credit to be an outsized driver of growth" citing partner managers, Brookfield Wealth Solutions allocations, and "we just put Oaktree and Brookfield together."
  • Daniel F. Welden, Wells Fargo: Asked about scaling the capital markets build-out and where Brookfield will/won’t participate; CEO Teskey: "We've already made the investments... as the revenue grows from here, we expect it to be very high margin" and "the growth driver... is... our increasing involvement in the capital markets activities of our own portfolio companies."
  • Michael Cyprys, Morgan Stanley: Asked what risks long-term AI contracts do not protect against and what could cause missed returns; CEO Teskey: "We take corporate credit counterparty risks" and "operating and construction risk" and said Brookfield invests only against contracts backed by "the largest, best corporate credit counterparties... or sovereigns."
  • Daniel Fannon, Jefferies: Asked about private wealth product roadmap over 1-2 years; CEO Teskey: "We do have a very robust pipeline of new products" including scaling private equity and real estate private wealth products and "a very healthy pipeline of new credit products... around asset-backed lending."
  • Crispin Love, Piper Sandler: Asked about ramp in net carried interest after earlier-than-expected realization; CFO Marshall: "these near-term realizations will remain episodic over the next couple of years" before a larger ramp (and cited realized carry drivers).
  • Michael Brown, UBS: Asked about credit fee-rate uptick and fee-bearing capital growth drivers for 2027; CEO Teskey: "we largely expect the fee rates on our credit products to remain very consistent" and highlighted a fee-bearing capital "huge step-up Jan 1" as the infrastructure flagship starts charging fees.
  • Jaeme Gloyn, National Bank Financial: Asked for thoughts on the election’s implications for energy; CEO Teskey: "the election results this week could potentially open up the possibility for either permitting reform or the extension of tax credits" while adding, "We're not banking on that in any way."

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts: Slightly negative to neutral, with repeated probing on AI downside (permitting, power sourcing, construction execution, demand durability), including questions framed around risks and crowding.
  • Management: Positive and confident in prepared remarks, with emphasis on resilience and scale; in Q&A, CEO Teskey used reinforcing language such as "we are treating AI infrastructure the exact same way" and "we don't put dollars in the ground until the permits are secured," while also noting uncertainty around policy outcomes ("it remains to be seen").
  • Versus last quarter: The current call’s Q&A stayed heavily centered on AI execution risk, while the prior quarter included more emphasis on large strategic items in prepared remarks (including the "$40 billion Just Group mandate") and more discussion of index classification mechanics around Oaktree.

Quarter-over-quarter Comparison

  • "The second quarter was exceptional... the quarter delivered $77 billion of fundraising." (CEO Teskey, prior quarter) vs. "We raised $123 billion in the first 3 quarters of the year, including $25 billion of capital in the third quarter." (CEO Teskey, current quarter)
  • "Fee-bearing capital reached $672 billion" (CEO Teskey, prior quarter) vs. "Fee-bearing capital reached $682 billion" (CEO Teskey, current quarter)
  • "Fee-related earnings... were $808 million" (CEO Teskey, prior quarter) vs. "third quarter fee-related earnings... $864 million" (CEO Teskey, current quarter)
  • "Beginning next quarter, our reported margins will reflect the completion of our Oaktree acquisition" (Chief Financial Officer Hadley Marshall, prior quarter) vs. "the completion of our acquisition of the remaining interest in Oaktree changes our consolidated margin" and "we expect margins to improve" (CFO Marshall, current quarter)
  • "we expect to begin generating and realizing carry earlier than we previously forecasted" (CEO Teskey, prior quarter) vs. "$48 million of net realized carry to BAM" and longer-dated carry targets (CFO Marshall, current quarter)

Risks and Concerns

  • "We'll begin charging fees in the fund as of January 1, a couple of months later than initially planned" creating timing-related fee recognition risk tied to deployment pacing. (CFO Marshall)
  • "With the share price down this year, we no longer expect to earn that fee in 2026" referencing the BBU high watermark mechanics and timing of performance fees. (CFO Marshall)
  • "We take corporate credit counterparty risks... And then operating and construction risk" as the key AI infrastructure risks management is underwriting, with mitigation framed as contracts with top-tier counterparties and Brookfield’s construction/operating capabilities. (CEO Teskey)

Final Takeaway

Management described Q3 2026 as another quarter of broad-based activity, highlighted by $682 billion of fee-bearing capital, $864 million of fee-related earnings, and the first meaningful post-spin carried interest realization ($48 million net to BAM). Executives pointed to infrastructure fundraising scale—$26 billion of commitments to date for the flagship Core Plus vintage with an expectation to exceed a $30 billion target in early 2027—while positioning AI infrastructure as a contracted, permit-secured development strategy and credit as an “outsized driver of growth,” supported by Oaktree and Brookfield Wealth Solutions flows. Timing items—January 1 fee start for the new infrastructure flagship and the loss of the BBU performance fee in 2026 due to the high watermark—were presented as affecting when fees are recorded rather than long-term earnings power.

data.title: AI stocks will ‘come back in vogue’ but AI data center buildout will slow after Democrat sweep – BofA
data.description:
BofA Global Research is warning that the “Democratic tsunami” in the 2026 U.S. midterms could significantly rattle risk assets, signaling what analysts describe as an "electoral shift from populist capitalism to populist socialism."

According to BofA, this shift would push taxes and regulations higher rather than lower, creating headwinds for corporate earnings and challenging the current "K-shape consumer boom" and AI capital expenditure surge that have powered markets.

BofA Global Research points to voter sentiment as a key driver of the political shift, with cost of living and AI infrastructure emerging as central concerns.

According to The Voter Poll conducted by SSRS, 89% of respondents cited cost of living as a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote, while 56% pointed to AI data centers as a significant issue.

BofA noted that "voters want cheaper cost of living, end war, slow AI data center expansion," suggesting political pressure will mount against the tech sector's aggressive buildout.

The data center backlash is already taking shape at the state level, according to BofA Global Research.

"Many incoming [Democrat] governors ran on 'stop the data centers' campaigns and are running key AI states," the analysts wrote, noting that approximately 1,400 data centers representing roughly 50 GW of existing capacity currently operate in the U.S.

With Texas accounting for 30% of anticipated capacity yet to break ground by 2028, BofA suggests the $2T AI capex forecast for 2028 is "a little too high." According to The Voter Poll, 76% of respondents oppose new data center construction in their communities.

BofA Global Research projected that the 2026 midterms will mark "peak AI equity concentration," triggering a rotation in market leadership.

The analysts recommend positioning toward "gold (XAUUSD:CUR) over oil (CO1:COM), (CL1:COM), lower yields (US10Y), (US2Y), (US30Y), tech bonds over tech stocks (XLK), consumer stocks (XLY), (XLP) over energy (XLE), small cap (IWM) over monopolies, long Europe (VGK), (FEZ), and long China tech (CQQQ)."

BofA noted that once bond yields reset lower without a recession, "AI stocks come back in vogue, but AI data center buildout at slower pace with more regulations/taxes."
